description: Cape of Good Hope, Calicut, the naming of America and the first circumnavigation of the globe.
content_html:
Bartolomeu Dias and the Cape of Good Hope, 1488

While Columbus was still trying to find a sponsor, the Portuguese had already made their most significant African breakthrough. In 1488, Bartolomeu Dias rounded the southern tip of Africa in stormy conditions, naming the headland the “Cape of Storms.” King John II of Portugal renamed it the “Cape of Good Hope” — because it offered hope of finding the sea route to India. Dias had solved the geographical puzzle that had blocked Portuguese progress for decades: Africa had an end, and beyond it lay the Indian Ocean.

Dias did not proceed to India on this voyage; his crew, exhausted after months at sea, mutinied and forced a return. He set up a stone pillar on the cape to mark Portugal’s claim and turned back. His contribution was crucial nonetheless: he proved the route was viable and provided the knowledge that made da Gama’s later voyage possible.

Key Fact

In 1488 Bartolomeu Dias became the first European to round the southern tip of Africa (Cape of Good Hope), proving a sea route to Asia existed — but his crew mutinied before he could reach India.

Vasco da Gama and the Route to India, 1497–1499

Vasco da Gama set out from Lisbon in July 1497 with four ships and about 170 men. He followed Dias’s route around the Cape of Good Hope, then crossed the Indian Ocean with the help of a local navigator (traditionally identified as Ahmed ibn Majid, though this attribution is disputed by some historians). In May 1498 he arrived at Calicut (modern Kozhikode) on the Malabar Coast of India — the heart of the spice trade.

Da Gama’s reception in Calicut was mixed. The Hindu ruler (the Zamorin) was unimpressed by the cloth and trinkets Portugal offered as trade goods; Arab merchants, whose profits would be cut by a new European sea route, worked to undermine Portuguese trade. Da Gama returned to Portugal in 1499 with a cargo of spices that more than repaid the cost of the expedition. Portugal had achieved its goal. A direct sea route from Europe to the spices of Asia was now open, bypassing the Ottoman-controlled overland routes entirely.

The direct sea route to India transformed European trade. Spice prices in Europe fell as Portuguese ships bypassed Arab and Ottoman middlemen. Lisbon became one of the wealthiest cities in Europe, replacing Venice (which had profited from overland trade) as the hub of the spice trade. The Portuguese established trading posts and fortified positions along the African and Indian coasts — the beginning of a maritime empire that stretched from Brazil to the Spice Islands. Da Gama made two further voyages to India (1502 and 1524), dying in Cochin (modern Kochi) in December 1524.

Amerigo Vespucci and the Naming of America

Amerigo Vespucci made at least two voyages to the South American coast (c.1499–1504). In letters that circulated widely in Europe — most notably the “Mundus Novus” (New World) letter of around 1502 — he argued that the lands Columbus had found were not part of Asia but a previously unknown continent. This was the crucial insight Columbus himself had refused to make. In 1507, the German cartographer Martin Waldseemüller published a world map labelling the new continent “America” in Vespucci’s honour — the first known use of the name. Columbus’s name was never attached to the continents he had reached first.

Key Fact

Amerigo Vespucci argued in his “Mundus Novus” letter (c.1502) that the Americas were a previously unknown continent, not part of Asia. German cartographer Martin Waldseemüller named the continent “America” after Vespucci on his 1507 world map.

Ferdinand Magellan and the First Circumnavigation, 1519–1522

Ferdinand Magellan was a Portuguese sailor who, after falling out with the Portuguese king, offered his services to Spain. His proposal: to find a westward route to the Spice Islands (the Moluccas) by sailing around the southern tip of South America. In September 1519 he departed from Seville with five ships and around 270 men.

The voyage was gruelling. Magellan navigated the treacherous passage at the southern tip of South America (now called the Strait of Magellan) in November 1520 and emerged into a vast, calm ocean he named the Pacific (“peaceful”). The crossing took ninety-nine days — far longer than expected. The crew ran out of food and were reduced to eating leather, rats and sawdust. When they finally reached Guam in March 1521 and the Philippines shortly afterwards, the relief was immense.

Magellan was killed in the Philippines on 27 April 1521, fighting alongside local allies in the Battle of Mactan. Command eventually passed to the Spanish navigator Juan Sebastián Elcano. By the time the expedition reached the Spice Islands and began the return journey across the Indian Ocean and around Africa, only one ship — the Victoria — and eighteen men from the original crew of around 270 survived. They arrived back in Seville on 6 September 1522. The circumnavigation proved definitively that the Earth was a sphere and that the Americas were entirely separate from Asia. Spain had failed to reach the Spice Islands cheaply by this route; the Pacific crossing was too long and costly.
exam_tip_html: Questions about the explorers often test the 8-mark “Explain Change” type: here you must explain what changed as a result of these voyages, not just describe what happened. Think about what changed for European trade routes (Lisbon replaced Venice), for geographical knowledge (confirmation that America was a separate continent; the Earth’s circumference confirmed by Magellan), and for indigenous populations. For 6-mark cause/consequence questions, always link your evidence directly to the specific cause or consequence you are explaining — examiners reward explicit causal links, not just description.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Bartolomeu Dias rounded the Cape of Good Hope in 1488, proving a sea route to Asia existed; Vasco da Gama completed the voyage to Calicut, India, in 1497–1499, opening direct European trade with Asia and making Lisbon Europe’s new trading hub.
  • Amerigo Vespucci recognised in his “Mundus Novus” letter (c.1502) that the Americas were a previously unknown continent; German cartographer Waldseemüller named the continent after him on his 1507 world map.
  • Magellan’s expedition (1519–1522) completed the first circumnavigation of the globe, proving the Earth was a sphere and the Americas were separate from Asia; Magellan was killed in the Philippines in 1521 and Elcano brought the surviving Victoria home in September 1522.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of Bartolomeu Dias’s 1488 voyage.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for identifying a feature (e.g. rounded the southern tip of Africa / named the Cape of Good Hope / crew mutinied and forced a return before reaching India). Two marks for a developed explanation of significance.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of Magellan’s circumnavigation of the globe, 1519–1522.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• He navigated the Strait of Magellan (southern tip of South America) in November 1520, providing the first European passage between the Atlantic and Pacific.
• He named the Pacific Ocean after its apparent calmness after the storms of the strait.
• He was killed at the Battle of Mactan in the Philippines on 27 April 1521; Elcano completed the voyage.
• Only eighteen of the original ~270 crew survived, arriving back in Seville on 6 September 1522.
[2 marks per feature: 1 for identification, 2 for development]

practice_questions.text: Explain one cause of Lisbon becoming Europe’s leading commercial city by the early sixteenth century.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies and develops a cause with evidence — e.g. da Gama’s opening of a direct sea route to India allowed Portuguese traders to buy spices at source and sell in Europe without paying Ottoman or Arab intermediaries; spice prices fell; wealth concentrated in Lisbon; links specifically to the 1497–1499 voyage and the displacement of Venice as the spice hub.
Secure: Identifies a cause with relevant supporting detail.
Developing: Names a cause with limited explanation.
Emerging: Vague statement without development.

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of Magellan’s circumnavigation for European geographical knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Explains that the circumnavigation proved definitively that the Earth was a sphere and that the Americas were entirely separate from Asia; links to the specific evidence of the 1519–1522 voyage; explains how this changed European understanding of the globe and enabled more accurate cartography.
Secure: Identifies consequence with supporting evidence.
Developing: States a consequence with basic explanation.
Emerging: Brief point without development.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of Vasco da Gama’s voyage to India (1497–1499).
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analyses significance at the time (first European sea voyage to India; cargo of spices repaid the cost many times over; undermined Arab and Ottoman trade monopoly; made Lisbon the centre of European trade) AND over time (established the Portuguese maritime empire from Brazil to the Spice Islands; transformed the global spice trade; reduced prices in Europe). Developed with evidence.
Secure: Addresses significance with evidence; may not fully develop the over-time dimension.
Developing: Describes what da Gama did without analysing significance.
Emerging: Brief or general points only.

practice_questions.text: 'Amerigo Vespucci’s contribution to the age of exploration was more significant than Bartolomeu Dias’s.' How far do you agree with this interpretation?
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments supporting the interpretation:
• Vespucci’s “Mundus Novus” letter (c.1502) established that the Americas were a new continent — the intellectual breakthrough that reframed the entire European understanding of the globe.
• The Americas were named after him, ensuring a lasting legacy in geographical knowledge.
• His recognition of a “New World” directly influenced subsequent expeditions and colonisation strategies.

Arguments challenging the interpretation:
• Dias’s rounding of the Cape of Good Hope in 1488 was the crucial practical breakthrough that made da Gama’s voyage and Portugal’s trading empire possible.
• Without Dias, the sea route to Asia might have remained theoretical; his voyage directly enabled the transformation of European trade.
• Vespucci’s exact role and the authenticity of some letters attributed to him have been questioned by historians.

Mastering: Sustained argument, agrees AND disagrees with evidence, reaches a substantiated judgement.
Secure: Clear argument with evidence on both sides.
Developing: Some relevant points, limited judgement.
Emerging: Descriptive, no evaluation of the interpretation.

flashcard_questions.q: When did Bartolomeu Dias round the Cape of Good Hope?
Why did Dias fail to reach India in 1488?
flashcard_questions.a: His crew mutinied and forced a return before they could proceed to India.

flashcard_questions.q: When did Vasco da Gama reach Calicut, India?
What was the significance of da Gama's voyage for European trade?
flashcard_questions.a: It opened a direct sea route to the spice trade, bypassing Ottoman-controlled overland routes.

flashcard_questions.q: Who named the Americas and in what year?
flashcard_questions.a: German cartographer Martin Waldseemüller named them on his 1507 world map, after Amerigo Vespucci.

flashcard_questions.q: What did Amerigo Vespucci argue in 'Mundus Novus' (c.1502)?
flashcard_questions.a: That the Americas were a previously unknown continent, not part of Asia.

flashcard_questions.q: When did Magellan's expedition depart from Seville?
What is the Strait of Magellan?
flashcard_questions.a: The treacherous passage at the southern tip of South America linking the Atlantic and Pacific oceans.

flashcard_questions.q: What did Magellan name the vast ocean he entered in 1520?
When and where was Magellan killed?
flashcard_questions.a: 27 April 1521, at the Battle of Mactan in the Philippines.
Juan Sebastián Elcano, arriving back in Seville on 6 September 1522.

glossary_terms.definition: Portuguese explorer (c.1450–1500) who in 1488 became the first European to round the southern tip of Africa, opening the sea route to Asia.
Portuguese explorer (c.1460s–1524) who completed the first European sea voyage to India in 1497–1499, reaching Calicut on the Malabar Coast.
A major spice-trading port on the Malabar Coast of India (modern Kozhikode, Kerala), which was Vasco da Gama's destination in 1498.
Florentine explorer (1454–1512) who argued the Americas were a previously unknown continent; the continents are named after him.
Portuguese explorer (c.1480–1521) who led the first circumnavigation of the globe (1519–1522); killed in the Philippines in 1521.
Basque Spanish navigator (c.1486–1526) who completed the first circumnavigation of the globe in 1522 after Magellan's death.
